displacement is two rows down and two columns left per period: the highway runs to the south-west, at speed $2/104$ in each coordinate.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, path = {}, (0, 0), 0, [(0, 0)]
for _ in range(12_000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    path.append(p)
P = np.array(path)
s = next(s for s in range(12_000 - 1000) if (P[s + 104:s + 1000] - P[s:s + 896] == P[s + 104] - P[s]).all())
print("periodic from step", s, "; displacement per 104 steps:", (P[s + 104] - P[s]).tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
periodic from step 9976 ; displacement per 104 steps: [2, -2]
```
:::

The package's ant can be checked against the definition. The run compares the colours of a torus of $80 \times 80$ cells every $100$ steps.

::: {#exm-ant-package}
#### The package against the definition

`LangtonsAntSystem` and a direct implementation of the step agree on the colouring and the position of the ant at every recorded time up to $11\,000$ steps, on a torus large enough that
the transient does not wrap around.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import LangtonsAntSystem
L = 80
run = simulate(LangtonsAntSystem((L, L)), until=11_000)
colours = np.asarray(run.get_values("cells.color")).reshape(-1, L, L)
ants = np.asarray(run.get_values("cells.ant")).reshape(-1, L, L)
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
c, (i, j), h, agree = np.zeros((L, L), dtype=int), (L // 2, L // 2), 0, True
for t in range(1, 11_001):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if c[i, j] == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    c[i, j] ^= 1
    i, j = (i + D[h][0]) % L, (j + D[h][1]) % L
    if t % 100 == 0:
        agree &= bool((c == colours[t // 100]).all() and ants[t // 100, i, j] == h)
print("package and definition agree at all 110 recorded times:", agree)
```

```{.text .run-output}
package and definition agree at all 110 recorded times: True
```
:::

The sources use different conventions. Downey turns right on black and left on white; Charbonneau moves first and then turns
[@downeyThinkComplexity2018, Ch. 6, Exercise 6-5; @charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 2.4].

::: {#exm-ant-conventions}
#### Conventions

Exchanging the turns is the same as reflecting the lattice in a vertical line, which exchanges left and right: Downey's ant traces the mirror image of the trajectory of the definition, and
its highway runs to the south-east. Charbonneau's order "move, then paint and turn" cuts the same sequence of actions at a different place: his ant moves first, so its orbit is that of the
definition started one cell further along. In all versions the highway appears after a little more than $10^4$ steps [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 2.4].
:::

The highway leaves an ordered trail. Its colours repeat, so the number of black cells grows by a fixed amount per period.

::: {#exm-ant-black-cells}
#### Black cells along the highway

The number of black cells is $720$ at step $10\,000$ and grows by $12$ in every period of $104$ steps once the highway runs: each period paints a new stretch of road.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, black = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
for _ in range(12_000):
    v = colour.get(p, 0)
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - v
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    black.append(sum(colour.values()))
print("black cells at 10000, 11000, 12000:", black[9999], black[10999], black[11999], "; growth per period at the end:", black[11999] - black[11999 - 104])
```

```{.text .run-output}
black cells at 10000, 11000, 12000: 720 834 952 ; growth per period at the end: 12
```
:::

The highway is fragile. Charbonneau sprinkles a few random black cells before the start, and every time the ant hits one the road breaks into a disordered episode, after which a new
highway, possibly in another direction, starts [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 2.4, Fig. 2.11].

::: {#exm-ant-noise}
#### A noisy background

With one cell in $1000$ black at random, the ant below is followed for $60\,000$ steps. Its distance from the start, recorded every $10\,000$ steps, keeps growing: the ant still escapes, along
highways that are interrupted where it meets a black cell.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
rng, L = np.random.default_rng(16), 1001
base = (rng.random((L, L)) < 0.001).astype(int)
flips, p, h, far = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
for t in range(1, 60_001):
    v = base[p[0] % L, p[1] % L] ^ flips.get(p, 0)
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    if t % 10_000 == 0:
        far.append(max(abs(p[0]), abs(p[1])))
print("distance from the start every 10000 steps:", far)
```

```{.text .run-output}
distance from the start every 10000 steps: [16, 66, 202, 284, 402, 556]
```
:::

On a torus the highway eventually meets its own trail. Charbonneau describes the ant falling back into disorder, starting a new highway at right angles, and the lattice filling with
blotches of disorder [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 2.4].

::: {#exm-ant-torus}
#### Wrapping around a torus

On the $80 \times 80$ torus of the package, the share of black cells keeps growing over $30\,000$ steps, as stretches of highway and disordered blotches fill the torus.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import LangtonsAntSystem
run = simulate(LangtonsAntSystem((80, 80)), until=30_000, dt=5000)
print("share of black cells every 5000 steps:", np.round(np.asarray(run.get_values("cells.color")).mean(axis=1), 3).tolist())
```

```{.text .run-output}
share of black cells every 5000 steps: [0.0, 0.054, 0.112, 0.187, 0.242, 0.286, 0.314]
```
:::

The ant's step can be undone. The previous position is one cell behind the ant, and the colour it found there is the opposite of the present colour.

::: {#exm-ant-reversible}
#### Running the ant backwards

From $(c', p', h')$ the previous position is $p = p' - \mathbf e_{h'}$, the previous colour there is $1 - c'(p)$, and the previous heading is $h' - 1$ or $h' + 1$ according to that colour.
Running $5000$ steps forward and $5000$ backward returns the white lattice with the ant at the start, heading north.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h = {}, (0, 0), 0
for _ in range(5000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
for _ in range(5000):
    p = (p[0] - D[h][0], p[1] - D[h][1])
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    h = (h - 1) % 4 if colour[p] == 0 else (h + 1) % 4
print("back at the start:", p == (0, 0) and h == 0 and not any(colour.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
back at the start: True
```
:::

The moves of the ant alternate between the two axes. This simple fact is the key to the theorem of the next subsection.

::: {#exm-ant-axes}
#### Alternating axes

Every step changes the heading by $\pm1$, so north-south and east-west headings alternate, and so do vertical and horizontal moves. The parity of row plus column changes at every move. In the
first $12\,000$ steps, every cell with even row plus column is entered by a vertical move and every cell with odd row plus column by a horizontal one.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, axes = {}, (0, 0), 0, {}
for _ in range(12_000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    axes.setdefault((p[0] + p[1]) % 2, set()).add("vertical" if h % 2 == 0 else "horizontal")
print(axes)
```

```{.text .run-output}
{1: {'horizontal'}, 0: {'vertical'}}
```
:::

The initial colouring can be anything, finite or not. On a checkerboard the ant finds a straight road at once.

::: {#exm-ant-checkerboard}
#### A checkerboard

Started on the checkerboard colouring $c(i, j) = (i + j) \bmod 2$, the ant's distance from the start grows linearly from the beginning, by one cell every two steps, without any transient.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
flips, p, h, far = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
for t in range(1, 2001):
    v = (p[0] + p[1]) % 2 ^ flips.get(p, 0)
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    if t % 500 == 0:
        far.append(max(abs(p[0]), abs(p[1])))
print("distance every 500 steps:", far)
```

```{.text .run-output}
distance every 500 steps: [250, 500, 750, 1000]
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the heading convention of the package. North is row $-1$ and a white cell turns the ant right.

::: {#exr-ant-convention}
#### The package's first steps

Run `LangtonsAntSystem` with `dt=1` for four steps on a $9 \times 9$ torus and compare the ant's positions and headings with @exm-ant-first-steps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Starting from the middle cell $(4, 4)$ heading north, the definition gives the positions $(4, 5), (5, 5), (5, 4), (4, 4)$ with headings east, south, west, north, a square walked clockwise
on screen, since rows grow downwards. The package records the ant's heading in the cell it occupies.

## Python

The positions and headings in the package's record.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import LangtonsAntSystem
run = simulate(LangtonsAntSystem((9, 9)), until=4, dt=1)
ants = np.asarray(run.get_values("cells.ant")).reshape(-1, 9, 9)
for t in range(5):
    (i, j), = np.argwhere(ants[t] >= 0)
    print(t, (int(i), int(j)), "NESW"[int(ants[t, i, j])])
```

```{.text .run-output}
0 (4, 4) N
1 (4, 5) E
2 (5, 5) S
3 (5, 4) W
4 (4, 4) N
```
::::
:::

The second exercise proves that the step is invertible. The backward run of the examples is its algorithm.

::: {#exr-ant-inverse}
#### The step is a bijection

Show that the step of the definition is a bijection of the set of states, with the inverse of @exm-ant-reversible. Check on a random colouring of a torus that the inverse undoes $1000$ steps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Given $(c', p', h')$, the previous state must have $p = p' - \mathbf e_{h'}$, since the ant moved along $\mathbf e_{h'}$; it must have $c(p) = 1 - c'(p)$ and $c = c'$ elsewhere, since only $p$
was flipped; and it must have $h = h' - 1$ if $c(p) = 0$ and $h = h' + 1$ if $c(p) = 1$. These formulas define a map $B$ with $B \circ (\text{step}) = \mathrm{id}$, and the step applied to
$B(c', p', h')$ gives back $(c', p', h')$ by the same computation, so the step is a bijection with inverse $B$.

## Python

A $50 \times 50$ torus with random colours.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
L = 50
c0 = np.random.default_rng(17).integers(0, 2, (L, L))
c, (i, j), h = c0.copy(), (25, 25), 0
for _ in range(1000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if c[i, j] == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    c[i, j] ^= 1
    i, j = (i + D[h][0]) % L, (j + D[h][1]) % L
for _ in range(1000):
    i, j = (i - D[h][0]) % L, (j - D[h][1]) % L
    c[i, j] ^= 1
    h = (h - 1) % 4 if c[i, j] == 0 else (h + 1) % 4
print("initial state recovered:", bool((c == c0).all()) and (i, j, h) == (25, 25, 0))
```

```{.text .run-output}
initial state recovered: True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise checks the period of the highway in detail. The colours along the road repeat as well as the motion.

::: {#exr-ant-highway-colours}
#### The road repeats

Show that once the highway has started, the colouring in a window that moves with the ant, two cells per period, repeats every $104$ steps. Check it from step $10\,400$ on.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The ant's motion during a period depends only on the colours it reads, which are those of the cells near it. If the colours in a window around the ant at time $s$ equal those at time $s + 104$
translated by the displacement, and the cells ahead of the ant are white at both times, the next period is a translate of the previous one, and by induction the highway continues. The check
compares windows of $11 \times 11$ cells around the ant.

## Python

Windows around the ant at times $10\,400 + 104k$, translated back by $k$ displacements.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, snaps = {}, (0, 0), 0, {}
for t in range(1, 11_000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    if t >= 10_400 and (t - 10_400) % 104 == 0:
        snaps[t] = (p, np.array([[colour.get((p[0] + a, p[1] + b), 0) for b in range(-5, 6)] for a in range(-5, 6)]))
ref = snaps[10_400][1]
print("windows equal at every period:", all((w == ref).all() for _, w in snaps.values()), "; positions:", [q for q, _ in snaps.values()][:3])
```

```{.text .run-output}
windows equal at every period: True ; positions: [(0, -24), (2, -26), (4, -28)]
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise exploits the symmetry between colours. Starting on black instead of white mirrors the trajectory.

::: {#exr-ant-black-start}
#### Starting on black

Show that the ant started on an all-black lattice traces the mirror image, in the vertical axis through the start, of the trajectory started on white. Check the first $11\,000$ positions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Let $M$ be the reflection $(i, j) \mapsto (i, -j)$, acting on colourings, positions and headings, where it exchanges east and west. If $(c_t, p_t, h_t)$ is the orbit from white, then $(1 - Mc_t,
Mp_t, Mh_t)$ is the orbit from black. Indeed, the reflected ant reads the colour $1 - c_t(p_t)$, so it turns the other way, and a reflection turns a right turn into a left turn, so its new heading is
$M h_{t + 1}$; it flips the cell $Mp_t$ and moves along $\mathbf e_{Mh_{t + 1}}$ to $Mp_{t + 1}$. So the positions from black are the mirror images of those from white.

## Python

The two runs, the second compared with the reflection $j \mapsto -j$.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
def path(background, n=11_000):
    flips, p, h, out = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
    for _ in range(n):
        v = background ^ flips.get(p, 0)
        h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
        flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
        p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
        out.append(p)
    return out
white, black = path(0), path(1)
print("black path is the mirror image:", all(b == (a[0], -a[1]) for a, b in zip(white, black)))
```

```{.text .run-output}
black path is the mirror image: True
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise asks how often the ant comes back. During the transient it passes the origin repeatedly, during the highway never.

::: {#exr-ant-returns}
#### Returns to the start

Count the returns of the ant to its starting cell in the first $12\,000$ steps and find the last one. Explain why there is a last one, using the highway.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Once the highway runs, the ant's position after the start $s$ of the highway is within a bounded distance of the line $p_s + k(2, -2)$, so its distance from the origin grows linearly and it never
returns. The returns all happen in the transient; the run finds $28$, the last at step $8068$.

## Python

The returns, from the direct implementation.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, returns = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
for t in range(1, 12_001):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    if p == (0, 0):
        returns.append(t)
print(len(returns), "returns; the last at step", returns[-1])
```

```{.text .run-output}
28 returns; the last at step 8068
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise measures the size of the disordered blob. It grows slowly before the highway.

::: {#exr-ant-blob}
#### The size of the transient

Record the largest distance of the ant from its start, in the $\ell_\infty$ norm, up to steps $1000, 5000, 9000, 10\,000, 11\,000$ and $12\,000$. How fast does it grow before and after the highway
starts?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Before the highway the blob grows irregularly and slowly: about $30$ cells in $9000$ steps. After it, the distance grows by $2$ cells per $104$ steps, about $20$ per $1000$ steps, which the last
two values show.

## Python

The running maximum of the distance.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, far, best = {}, (0, 0), 0, {}, 0
for t in range(1, 12_001):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    best = max(best, abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]))
    if t in (1000, 5000, 9000, 10_000, 11_000, 12_000):
        far[t] = best
print(far)
```

```{.text .run-output}
{1000: 11, 5000: 22, 9000: 29, 10000: 29, 11000: 37, 12000: 57}
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise changes the initial heading. The rule is symmetric under rotations of the lattice.

::: {#exr-ant-heading}
#### Other initial headings

Show that starting the ant heading east, south or west on white rotates the whole trajectory by $90°$, $180°$ or $270°$. In which directions do the highways run? Check with `heading=1` in the package.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A rotation $\rho$ of the lattice about the start maps headings $h$ to $h + 1$ and preserves the white colouring and the turn rule, so it maps orbits to orbits: the orbit from heading $1$ is $\rho$ of the
orbit from heading $0$. The highway, which runs south-west from heading north, runs north-west from heading east, north-east from south and south-east from west. After $11\,000$ steps the ant
started north is $14$ rows down and $34$ columns left of the start, and the one started east is $34$ rows up and $14$ columns left: the first position rotated by $90°$.

## Python

Positions after $11\,000$ steps in the package for headings $0$ and $1$, relative to the start.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.computer_science.automata import LangtonsAntSystem
for heading in (0, 1):
    run = simulate(LangtonsAntSystem((100, 100), heading=heading), until=11_000, dt=11_000)
    (i, j), = np.argwhere(np.asarray(run.get_values("cells.ant"))[-1].reshape(100, 100) >= 0)
    print(f"heading {heading}: position relative to the start {(int(i) - 50, int(j) - 50)}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
heading 0: position relative to the start (14, -34)
heading 1: position relative to the start (-34, -14)
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise counts states on a torus. The count shows why every orbit there is periodic.

::: {#exr-ant-torus-states}
#### The state space of a torus

How many states does the ant have on an $L \times L$ torus? Using @exr-ant-inverse, show that every state lies on a cycle, so that the ant started on white returns to the white torus, at its start,
heading north.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

A state is a colouring, a position and a heading: $2^{L^2}L^2 \cdot 4$ states. A bijection of a finite set is a permutation, which is a product of cycles, so every state lies on a cycle, and the orbit of
the initial state returns to it. The return times found by a direct run are $8, 66, 96, 11\,710$ and $4592$ for $L = 2, \dots, 6$.

## Python

Direct runs until the initial state recurs.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
for L in range(2, 7):
    c, i, j, h, t = [[0] * L for _ in range(L)], 0, 0, 0, 0
    while True:
        h = (h + 1) % 4 if c[i][j] == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
        c[i][j] ^= 1
        i, j, t = (i + D[h][0]) % L, (j + D[h][1]) % L, t + 1
        if (i, j, h) == (0, 0, 0) and not any(map(any, c)):
            break
    print(f"L = {L}: {2 ** (L * L) * L * L * 4} states, return after {t} steps")
```

```{.text .run-output}
L = 2: 256 states, return after 8 steps
L = 3: 18432 states, return after 66 steps
L = 4: 4194304 states, return after 96 steps
L = 5: 3355443200 states, return after 11710 steps
L = 6: 9895604649984 states, return after 4592 steps
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise compares backgrounds. The theorem of the next subsection covers all of them; the behaviour differs.

::: {#exr-ant-backgrounds}
#### Random backgrounds

Run the ant for $200\,000$ steps on random colourings with black densities $0.1$, $0.5$ and $0.9$, and record its distance from the start every $50\,000$ steps. Compare with the highway's linear
growth.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

On a random background the ant keeps meeting colours it did not paint, and no highway lasts. Its distance after $200\,000$ steps is a few hundred cells, much less than the $4000$ or so that a highway
would cover, and it fluctuates rather than growing steadily. The colouring is generated on a large torus and read periodically, which for these distances is the same as an infinite random colouring.

## Python

Three backgrounds, one seed.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
rng, L = np.random.default_rng(18), 4001
for density in (0.1, 0.5, 0.9):
    base = (rng.random((L, L)) < density).astype(np.uint8)
    flips, p, h, far = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
    for t in range(1, 200_001):
        v = int(base[p[0] % L, p[1] % L]) ^ flips.get(p, 0)
        h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
        flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
        p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
        if t % 50_000 == 0:
            far.append(max(abs(p[0]), abs(p[1])))
    print(f"density {density}: distance every 50000 steps {far}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
density 0.1: distance every 50000 steps [56, 140, 174, 276]
density 0.5: distance every 50000 steps [40, 292, 692, 818]
density 0.9: distance every 50000 steps [78, 120, 26, 144]
```
::::
:::

The last exercise looks at the speed of the highway. It is the quantity of the speed of light of @prp-life-patterns for an agent.

::: {#exr-ant-speed}
#### The speed of the highway

The highway moves the ant by $(2, -2)$ every $104$ steps. Find its speed in the $\ell_\infty$ and Euclidean norms, and the number of steps after which the ant is $1000$ cells from its start in the
$\ell_\infty$ norm, ignoring the transient.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The speed is $2/104 = 1/52 \approx 0.0192$ cells per step in the $\ell_\infty$ norm and $2\sqrt2/104 \approx 0.0272$ in the Euclidean norm. A distance of $1000$ needs $500$ periods, $52\,000$ steps.
The ant, which can move one cell per step, uses only about $2\%$ of that speed on the highway.

## Python

The two speeds and the time.

```{.python .run}
import math
print(round(2 / 104, 4), round(2 * math.sqrt(2) / 104, 4), 500 * 104)
```

```{.text .run-output}
0.0192 0.0272 52000
```
::::
:::
::::

### The ant always escapes

Whether the ant eventually builds a highway from every finite initial colouring is an open problem (a literature statement). A weaker statement has a short proof, due to
Bunimovich and Troubetzkoy (a theorem of the literature, proved here in full): whatever the initial colouring, finite or infinite, the ant visits infinitely many cells. The
proof uses only the alternation of the axes of @exm-ant-axes and the alternation of the colour of a cell between visits; it also gives the invertibility of the step, which
makes every orbit on a torus periodic.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-ant-unbounded}
#### The trajectory of Langton's ant is unbounded

Consider Langton's ant on $\mathbb Z^2$ with an arbitrary initial colouring.

(a) The ant's moves alternate between vertical and horizontal, and the axis of the move by which the ant enters a cell depends only on the parity of the cell's row plus column.

(b) Between two consecutive visits to a cell, its colour is flipped exactly once, so the ant turns right and left on alternate visits.

(c) The step is a bijection of the set of states.

(d) The trajectory is unbounded.
:::

::::

*Proof.* (a) Each step changes the heading by $\pm1$ modulo $4$, so the headings alternate between the even ones, north and south, and the odd ones, east and west, and so do the axes
of the moves, which follow the new heading. Every move changes row plus column by $\pm1$, so its parity at time $t$ is that of $p_0$ plus $t$. The axis of the move at step $t$ and
the parity of the cell $p_t$ it enters are both determined by the parity of $t$, so the axis is a function of the parity of the cell.

(b) A cell is flipped exactly when the ant leaves it, so between two consecutive visits it is flipped once, at the end of the first. The ant reads opposite colours on consecutive visits
and turns the other way.

(c) This is @exr-ant-inverse.

(d) Suppose the trajectory is bounded. Then it visits finitely many cells, infinitely often in total, so the set $V$ of cells visited infinitely often is finite and nonempty, and after
some time $T_0$ the ant visits only cells of $V$. Let $X$ be the cell of $V$ with the smallest row (the northernmost row), and among those the largest column (the easternmost). Its
northern neighbour and its eastern neighbour are not in $V$. By (a), all entries into $X$ are along one axis.

If they are vertical, an entry heading south comes from the northern neighbour, which is visited only finitely often; so after some time every entry into $X$ heads north. At the next
step the ant turns right or left, to east or west, and by (b) these alternate between consecutive visits. So infinitely often the ant leaves $X$ to the east, into the eastern neighbour,
which is then visited infinitely often, a contradiction.

If the entries are horizontal, an entry heading west comes from the eastern neighbour, so after some time every entry heads east, and the exits alternate between south and north. Infinitely
often the ant leaves to the north, into the northern neighbour, again a contradiction. $\square$

Part (d) says nothing about the highway: it rules out confinement, not disorder. On a torus the lattice is finite and the trajectory is trivially bounded; there part (c) shows that the
orbit is a cycle through the initial state (@exr-ant-torus-states), the opposite of escape.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example looks at the cell used in the proof. On a white lattice it is easy to find the cells visited most during the transient.

::: {#exm-unb-turns-alternate}
#### Turns at one cell

At the starting cell, the ant's turns on its $29$ visits in the first $12\,000$ steps alternate exactly between right and left, as part (b) says, starting with a right turn on white.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, turns = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
for _ in range(12_000):
    v = colour.get(p, 0)
    if p == (0, 0):
        turns.append("R" if v == 0 else "L")
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - v
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
print("".join(turns), len(turns))
```

```{.text .run-output}
RLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLRLR 29
```
:::

Part (a) can be seen on any colouring. On a random colouring the entries into cells of each parity are all along one axis.

::: {#exm-unb-axes-random}
#### Axes on a random colouring

On a random colouring of density $\frac12$, over $50\,000$ steps, cells with even row plus column are entered only by vertical moves and cells with odd row plus column only by horizontal
ones, as on the white lattice.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
L = 1001
base = np.random.default_rng(19).integers(0, 2, (L, L))
flips, p, h, axes = {}, (0, 0), 0, {0: set(), 1: set()}
for _ in range(50_000):
    v = int(base[p[0] % L, p[1] % L]) ^ flips.get(p, 0)
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    axes[(p[0] + p[1]) % 2].add("vertical" if h % 2 == 0 else "horizontal")
print(axes)
```

```{.text .run-output}
{0: {'vertical'}, 1: {'horizontal'}}
```
:::

Escaping does not mean moving fast. On a random colouring the ant wanders far less than on the highway, but the theorem still says that it never settles into a bounded region.

::: {#exm-unb-escape-random}
#### Escape on a random background

On the random colouring of the previous example, the largest distance reached grows over $400\,000$ steps, recorded every $100\,000$ steps, far more slowly than the highway's $2$ cells per
$104$ steps.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
L = 1001
base = np.random.default_rng(19).integers(0, 2, (L, L))
flips, p, h, best, record = {}, (0, 0), 0, 0, []
for t in range(1, 400_001):
    v = int(base[p[0] % L, p[1] % L]) ^ flips.get(p, 0)
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    best = max(best, abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]))
    if t % 100_000 == 0:
        record.append(best)
print("largest distance so far, every 100000 steps:", record)
```

```{.text .run-output}
largest distance so far, every 100000 steps: [300, 442, 490, 490]
```
:::

On a torus the conclusion of part (d) fails, and part (c) gives the opposite. The ant returns to its exact initial state.

::: {#exm-unb-torus-return}
#### Return on a small torus

On the $3 \times 3$ torus the ant started on white, heading north, returns to the white torus at its start after $66$ steps (@exr-ant-torus-states). In between it visits every cell; the run
lists how many times.

```{.python .run}
import collections
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
L = 3
c, (i, j), h, visits = [[0] * L for _ in range(L)], (0, 0), 0, collections.Counter()
for t in range(66):
    visits[(i, j)] += 1
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if c[i][j] == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    c[i][j] ^= 1
    i, j = (i + D[h][0]) % L, (j + D[h][1]) % L
print("back at the start:", (i, j, h) == (0, 0, 0) and not any(map(any, c)), "; visits per cell:", sorted(visits.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
back at the start: True ; visits per cell: [6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 10, 10, 10]
```
:::

The extreme cell of the proof is a corner of the visited set. During the highway phase the visited set keeps acquiring new corners, which is how the ant escapes.

::: {#exm-unb-corner}
#### The northern-eastern corner

For the white lattice, the cell with the smallest row and, among those, the largest column of the set of cells visited in the first $t$ steps changes over time; after the highway starts, the
ant moves south-west, so the corner stops changing and the southern-western corner moves instead.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, visited = {}, (0, 0), 0, {(0, 0)}
for t in range(1, 12_001):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    visited.add(p)
    if t in (2000, 6000, 10_000, 12_000):
        ne = min(visited, key=lambda q: (q[0], -q[1]))
        sw = max(visited, key=lambda q: (q[0], -q[1]))
        print(f"t = {t}: north-east corner {ne}, south-west corner {sw}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
t = 2000: north-east corner (-14, 3), south-west corner (6, -3)
t = 6000: north-east corner (-16, 19), south-west corner (17, 20)
t = 10000: north-east corner (-22, 11), south-west corner (22, 19)
t = 12000: north-east corner (-22, 11), south-west corner (34, -53)
```
:::

The choice of the extreme cell matters. A cell that is extreme in only one direction does not give a contradiction.

::: {#exm-unb-why-corner}
#### Why a corner

If $X$ were only a northernmost cell of $V$, the eastern neighbour could be in $V$, and the exits to the east in the vertical case would be harmless. Taking the easternmost cell of the northernmost
row makes both the northern and the eastern neighbour lie outside $V$, which covers both axes of entry. Any corner works: the southern-western one with the opposite headings, for instance.
:::

Mirror conventions obey the same theorem. Downey's ant, which turns left on white, is the reflection of the ant of the definition.

::: {#exm-unb-mirror}
#### The theorem for other conventions

The reflection $M$ of @exr-ant-black-start maps orbits of the ant of the definition, started on any colouring $c$, to orbits of the mirror-image ant started on $Mc$, and maps bounded
trajectories to bounded trajectories. Applying part (d) to $M^{-1}c$ proves it for Downey's ant on $c$.
:::

The highway is a sufficient reason for escape but not a necessary one. The theorem covers colourings on which no highway is ever seen.

::: {#exm-unb-no-highway}
#### Escape without a highway

On the random backgrounds of @exr-ant-backgrounds no stretch of $104$-periodic motion lasts long, yet by part (d) the ant leaves every bounded region. On the checkerboard of
@exm-ant-checkerboard the ant moves away linearly from the first step, along a road different from the highway.
:::

Whether a highway always appears is open. The highway conjecture asserts it for every finite initial colouring (a literature statement), and part (d) is the strongest general statement
proved here.

::: {#exm-unb-highway-conjecture}
#### The highway conjecture

For the white lattice the highway is found by simulation after $9976$ steps (@exm-ant-highway), and for random finite perturbations Charbonneau's simulation shows highways restarting after each
disordered episode [@charbonneauNaturalComplexityModeling2017, Sec. 2.4, Fig. 2.11]. A proof for all finite colourings would need control of the disordered phase, which part (d) avoids by
arguing only about the cells visited infinitely often.
:::

The proof uses two colours only through the alternation of turns at a cell. For ants with more colours that cycle at each visit, what matters is whether both kinds of turn occur in
the cycle.

::: {#exm-unb-generalised}
#### Ants with more colours

An ant with three colours cycling $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 0$ and turns right, left, right turns at a cell in the repeating pattern $RLR$. In the vertical case of the proof an entry heading north is then
followed, on every third visit at least, by an exit to the east, and in the horizontal case by an exit to the north, so the proof of part (d) goes through. An ant that only ever turns right walks around a
$2 \times 2$ square forever, and its trajectory is bounded; the run shows both.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
for name, turn in (("RLR", {0: 1, 1: -1, 2: 1}), ("RRR", {0: 1, 1: 1, 2: 1})):
    colour, p, h, best = {}, (0, 0), 0, 0
    for t in range(100_000):
        v = colour.get(p, 0)
        h = (h + turn[v]) % 4
        colour[p] = (v + 1) % 3
        p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
        best = max(best, abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]))
    print(f"{name}: largest distance in 100000 steps {best}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
RLR: largest distance in 100000 steps 60
RRR: largest distance in 100000 steps 1
```
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise proves part (a) for colourings in general. The computation tests it on many random colourings.

::: {#exr-unb-axes}
#### Alternation of axes

Prove part (a) in detail, including the statement that the ant enters cells of one parity only by vertical moves. Check it on ten random colourings of density $0.3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The heading after step $t$ is $h_0 + \sum_{s \leq t}\epsilon_s \pmod 4$ with $\epsilon_s = \pm1$, so its parity is that of $h_0 + t$, and the move at step $t$ is vertical iff $h_0 + t$ is even. The
position after step $t$ has row plus column of the parity of $r_0 + c_0 + t$. So the move into $p_t$ is vertical iff $h_0 + t$ is even iff the parity of $p_t$ equals that of $r_0 + c_0 + h_0$.

## Python

Ten colourings, $20\,000$ steps each, and the set of axes seen per parity.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
rng, L, ok = np.random.default_rng(20), 501, True
for _ in range(10):
    base = (rng.random((L, L)) < 0.3).astype(int)
    flips, p, h, axes = {}, (0, 0), 0, {0: set(), 1: set()}
    for _ in range(20_000):
        v = int(base[p[0] % L, p[1] % L]) ^ flips.get(p, 0)
        h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
        flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
        p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
        axes[(p[0] + p[1]) % 2].add(h % 2)
    ok &= axes == {0: {0}, 1: {1}}
print("even cells entered vertically and odd cells horizontally in all runs:", ok)
```

```{.text .run-output}
even cells entered vertically and odd cells horizontally in all runs: True
```
::::
:::

The second exercise checks part (b) on a random colouring. The alternation must hold for every cell.

::: {#exr-unb-alternation}
#### Alternation of turns at every cell

Record the sequence of turns at each visited cell over $30\,000$ steps on a random colouring, and check that every sequence alternates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

By part (b) consecutive visits to a cell read opposite colours, so the turns alternate. The first turn depends on the initial colour of the cell, which on a random colouring varies from cell to cell.

## Python

The sequences of turns per cell.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
L = 501
base = np.random.default_rng(21).integers(0, 2, (L, L))
flips, p, h, seq = {}, (0, 0), 0, {}
for _ in range(30_000):
    v = int(base[p[0] % L, p[1] % L]) ^ flips.get(p, 0)
    seq.setdefault(p, []).append(v)
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if v == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    flips[p] = flips.get(p, 0) ^ 1
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
print(len(seq), "cells; all alternate:", all(all(a != b for a, b in zip(s, s[1:])) for s in seq.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
8820 cells; all alternate: True
```
::::
:::

The third exercise asks for the variant of the proof with another corner. The argument is symmetric.

::: {#exr-unb-other-corner}
#### The south-west corner

Rewrite the proof of part (d) with $X$ the cell of $V$ with the largest row and, among those, the smallest column. Which neighbours are outside $V$, and which entries become impossible?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The southern and western neighbours of $X$ are outside $V$. Vertical entries heading north come from the south and are finitely many, so eventually all entries head south, and the exits alternate
between west and east; the western exits enter a cell outside $V$ infinitely often. Horizontal entries heading east come from the west, so eventually all head west, and the exits alternate between
north and south; the southern ones give the contradiction.

## Python

A check of the case analysis: for each entry heading, the two possible exits after a right and a left turn.

```{.python .run}
names = "NESW"
for entry in range(4):
    print(f"entering heading {names[entry]}: exits {names[(entry + 1) % 4]} (right turn) or {names[(entry - 1) % 4]} (left turn)")
```

```{.text .run-output}
entering heading N: exits E (right turn) or W (left turn)
entering heading E: exits S (right turn) or N (left turn)
entering heading S: exits W (right turn) or E (left turn)
entering heading W: exits N (right turn) or S (left turn)
```
::::
:::

The fourth exercise shows that part (d) needs the plane. On a cylinder the ant can be confined.

::: {#exr-unb-cylinder}
#### A cylinder

On a cylinder $\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z_L$, periodic in the columns, which step of the proof of part (d) fails? Run the ant on white cylinders of widths $L = 2, \dots, 6$, record the range of rows it
visits, and for the widths where it stays confined find a repeated state, which proves that it stays confined forever.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

With columns periodic there is no easternmost cell in a row: the eastern neighbour of the chosen cell $X$ may lie in $V$, and neither case of the proof yields a contradiction. The conclusion fails too.
On the cylinders of widths $2$ and $4$ the state of the ant (position, heading and black cells) recurs, after $8$ and $96$ steps, so the motion is periodic and the trajectory bounded forever. On widths
$3$ and $5$ the ant moves thousands of rows along the cylinder in the run; on width $6$ it stays within $30$ rows, with no recurrence found in the first $2000$ steps, and the run decides nothing.

## Python

The range of rows in $50\,000$ steps, and for each width the first recurrence of the full state within $2000$ steps.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
for L in range(2, 7):
    colour, (i, j), h, rows, seen, period = {}, (0, 0), 0, [], {}, None
    for t in range(50_000):
        if t < 2000 and period is None:
            key = (i, j, h, tuple(sorted(k for k, v in colour.items() if v)))
            period = t - seen[key] if key in seen else None
            seen[key] = seen.get(key, t)
        h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get((i, j), 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
        colour[(i, j)] = 1 - colour.get((i, j), 0)
        i, j = i + D[h][0], (j + D[h][1]) % L
        rows.append(i)
    print(f"L = {L}: rows from {min(rows)} to {max(rows)}; state recurs with period {period}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
L = 2: rows from 0 to 1; state recurs with period 8
L = 3: rows from -1 to 8333; state recurs with period None
L = 4: rows from -1 to 2; state recurs with period 96
L = 5: rows from -2998 to 4; state recurs with period None
L = 6: rows from -13 to 16; state recurs with period None
```
::::
:::

The fifth exercise uses part (c) on a torus with a random colouring. Every state returns, whatever the colouring.

::: {#exr-unb-torus-random}
#### Return from a random colouring

On a $3 \times 3$ torus with a random initial colouring, find the time after which the initial state recurs, and check that the ant's trajectory before that time visits each cell.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The state space is finite and the step is a bijection by part (c), so the orbit of any state is a cycle through it; the run finds its length. That every cell is visited is a fact of the run, not a
consequence of the proposition.

## Python

Five random colourings of the $3 \times 3$ torus.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
L, rng = 3, np.random.default_rng(22)
for _ in range(5):
    c0 = rng.integers(0, 2, (L, L))
    c, (i, j), h, t, seen = c0.copy(), (0, 0), 0, 0, set()
    while True:
        seen.add((i, j))
        h = (h + 1) % 4 if c[i, j] == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
        c[i, j] ^= 1
        i, j, t = (i + D[h][0]) % L, (j + D[h][1]) % L, t + 1
        if (i, j, h) == (0, 0, 0) and (c == c0).all():
            break
    print(f"return after {t} steps, {len(seen)} cells visited")
```

```{.text .run-output}
return after 70 steps, 9 cells visited
return after 42 steps, 9 cells visited
return after 74 steps, 9 cells visited
return after 70 steps, 9 cells visited
return after 70 steps, 9 cells visited
```
::::
:::

The sixth exercise measures how long the ant stays in a box. By part (d) it leaves every box for good only if it builds a road out; it must at least leave every box.

::: {#exr-unb-exit-times}
#### Leaving boxes

For the white lattice, find for $R = 5, 10, 20, 40$ the first time the ant leaves the box $\lVert p\rVert_\infty \leq R$ and the last time it is inside it during the first $12\,000$ steps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (d) guarantees a first exit from every box, for any colouring. The last time inside is finite here because of the highway: once it runs, the distance grows linearly. For $R = 40$ the ant has
left only after the highway started, since the blob of the transient reaches only about $30$ cells.

## Python

First exit and last presence for each box.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, dist = {}, (0, 0), 0, [0]
for _ in range(12_000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    dist.append(max(abs(p[0]), abs(p[1])))
for R in (5, 10, 20, 40):
    first = next(t for t, d in enumerate(dist) if d > R)
    last = max(t for t, d in enumerate(dist) if d <= R)
    print(f"R = {R}: first exit at {first}, last time inside {last}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
R = 5: first exit at 224, last time inside 8487
R = 10: first exit at 901, last time inside 9240
R = 20: first exit at 3853, last time inside 10388
R = 40: first exit at 11149, last time inside 11428
```
::::
:::

The seventh exercise extends part (c) to more general agents. Reversibility holds whenever the rule can be read back.

::: {#exr-unb-reversible-general}
#### When is a turmite reversible

Consider an ant with colours $0, \dots, k - 1$ that on colour $v$ turns by $\theta(v) \in \{-1, 0, 1, 2\}$ and replaces $v$ by $\pi(v)$, then moves forward. Show that the step is a bijection when $\pi$
is a permutation. Check it for the three-colour ant of @exm-unb-generalised by running it forward and back.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

From the state after a step, the previous position is one cell behind the ant along its heading, the previous colour there is $\pi^{-1}$ of the present one, and the previous heading is the present one
minus $\theta$ of that previous colour. These determine the previous state uniquely and define an inverse, as in @exr-ant-inverse; if $\pi$ were not injective, two colours would give the same
successor and the previous colour could not be read back.

## Python

Forward $3000$ steps with $\pi(v) = v + 1 \bmod 3$ and turns right, left, right, then back.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
turn = {0: 1, 1: -1, 2: 1}
colour, p, h = {}, (0, 0), 0
for _ in range(3000):
    v = colour.get(p, 0)
    h = (h + turn[v]) % 4
    colour[p] = (v + 1) % 3
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
for _ in range(3000):
    p = (p[0] - D[h][0], p[1] - D[h][1])
    colour[p] = (colour[p] - 1) % 3
    h = (h - turn[colour[p]]) % 4
print("initial state recovered:", p == (0, 0) and h == 0 and not any(colour.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
initial state recovered: True
```
::::
:::

The eighth exercise turns part (d) into a quantitative statement. Since the motion inside a box depends only on the colours in the box, the ant cannot stay in it for long.

::: {#exr-unb-exit-bound}
#### A uniform bound on exit times

Show that whatever the colouring, the ant leaves the box $\lVert p - p_0\rVert_\infty \leq R$ within $N_R = 4(2R + 1)^22^{(2R + 1)^2}$ steps. For $R = 1$, find the longest time the ant can stay
in the box over all $512$ colourings of its cells and the four initial headings.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

While the ant is inside the box its steps depend only on the colours of the box, its position and its heading: $N_R$ possible box states. If it stayed inside for $N_R$ steps, two box states would
coincide, and by determinism the ant would repeat the same moves forever without leaving the box, a bounded trajectory, contradicting part (d). For $R = 1$ the bound is $4 \cdot 9 \cdot 512 = 18\,432$,
while the exhaustive search below finds a far smaller longest stay.

## Python

All colourings of the $3 \times 3$ box and all headings, with the ant at its centre.

```{.python .run}
import itertools
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
longest = 0
for bits in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=9):
    for h0 in range(4):
        c = {(a, b): bits[3 * (a + 1) + b + 1] for a in (-1, 0, 1) for b in (-1, 0, 1)}
        p, h, t = (0, 0), h0, 0
        while max(abs(p[0]), abs(p[1])) <= 1:
            h = (h + 1) % 4 if c[p] == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
            c[p] ^= 1
            p, t = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1]), t + 1
        longest = max(longest, t)
print("longest stay in the 3 x 3 box:", longest, "steps; bound", 4 * 9 * 512)
```

```{.text .run-output}
longest stay in the 3 x 3 box: 15 steps; bound 18432
```
::::
:::

The ninth exercise asks what part (d) says about returns. A bounded trajectory would return to some cell infinitely often; the theorem rules out boundedness, not returns.

::: {#exr-unb-finitely-many-returns}
#### Returns are not controlled

Does part (d) imply that every cell is visited only finitely often? Explain which step of the proof uses boundedness, and check that on the white lattice the ant eventually leaves the cells of its
transient for good.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

The proof needs all visits to lie in $V$ after some time, which uses boundedness; an unbounded trajectory may visit a finite set $V$ infinitely often and also wander far away in between. Part (d) excludes
only that the whole trajectory stays in a bounded set, so it does not imply finitely many visits to each cell. For the white lattice the highway gives finitely many returns ($28$ in @exr-ant-returns);
whether some colouring gives infinitely many returns together with an unbounded trajectory is not settled by the proposition.

## Python

The set of cells visited during the last $1000$ of $12\,000$ steps on the white lattice and its overlap with the cells visited before step $9000$: none, the ant has left.

```{.python .run}
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
colour, p, h, path = {}, (0, 0), 0, []
for _ in range(12_000):
    h = (h + 1) % 4 if colour.get(p, 0) == 0 else (h - 1) % 4
    colour[p] = 1 - colour.get(p, 0)
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
    path.append(p)
print("cells shared by the first 9000 and the last 1000 steps:", len(set(path[:9000]) & set(path[-1000:])))
```

```{.text .run-output}
cells shared by the first 9000 and the last 1000 steps: 0
```
::::
:::

The last exercise is about the number of colours. Part (b) is the only place where two colours are used.

::: {#exr-unb-where-two-colours}
#### Where the proof uses two colours

For an ant with colours $0, 1, 2$ cycling at each visit, show that the proof of part (d) still works for the turns right, right, left, and that both the proof and the conclusion fail for right, right,
right. Find the turn sequence at the most visited cell in a run of the first ant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
:::: {.panel-tabset .solution-tabs}
## Solution

Part (a) holds for any ant that turns by $\pm90°$ at every step, so entries into a cell are along one axis. In both cases of the proof, the contradiction needs an exit in the forbidden direction on
infinitely many visits. With turns $RRL$ repeating at a cell, an entry heading north is followed by exits east, east, west, and an entry heading east by exits south, south, north, so the forbidden
exits still occur on every third visit at least. With $RRR$ the ant turns right at every step and walks around a $2 \times 2$ square forever: a bounded trajectory, so no proof can exist.

## Python

The turn sequence at the most visited cell of a $20\,000$-step run of the $RRL$ ant.

```{.python .run}
import collections
D = [(-1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1)]
turn = {0: 1, 1: 1, 2: -1}
colour, p, h, seq = {}, (0, 0), 0, collections.defaultdict(list)
for _ in range(20_000):
    v = colour.get(p, 0)
    seq[p].append("R" if turn[v] == 1 else "L")
    h = (h + turn[v]) % 4
    colour[p] = (v + 1) % 3
    p = (p[0] + D[h][0], p[1] + D[h][1])
cell = max(seq, key=lambda q: len(seq[q]))
print(cell, "".join(seq[cell][:24]), len(seq[cell]))
```

```{.text .run-output}
(0, 0) RRLRRL 6
```
::::
:::
::::

## Random Boolean networks {#sec-boolean-networks}

A cellular automaton applies one rule on a regular lattice. Dropping both restrictions gives a Boolean network: binary variables, each updated by its own Boolean
function of a few other variables chosen anywhere in the system [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 6.3, (i)]. Kauffman introduced random networks of this kind in
the late 1960s as models of gene regulation, and proposed that the attractors of the network correspond to cell types
[@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.1]. Random Boolean networks are the standard benchmark of a complex system with many variables whose dynamics can still be
controlled: depending on the number $K$ of inputs per node they are frozen, critical or chaotic [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Secs. 7.1 and 7.3]. This section
defines them, computes their attractors, and proves the phase diagram of the annealed approximation, which places the transition at $K_c = 1/(2p(1 - p))$ and is the
quantitative content of "life at the edge of chaos".

For more on this topic, see @grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015 [Ch. 7].

### Boolean networks, attractors and basins

Gros describes a network by three choices: the connectivity $K_i$ of each element, its controlling elements, and its coupling function; with all $K_i = K$ and the
controlling elements drawn at random from the whole network, it is the $N$-$K$ model or Kauffman net [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.2.1]. The definition
adds the quenched, synchronous update that Gros uses for attractors [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.2.3].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-boolean-network}
#### Boolean network and the Kauffman model

A **Boolean network** on $N$ nodes assigns to each node $i$ a list of $K_i$ **controlling elements** $j_1(i), \dots, j_{K_i}(i)$ and a **coupling function** $f_i : \{0, 1\}^{K_i}
\to \{0, 1\}$, and updates the state $\boldsymbol\sigma = (\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_N) \in \{0, 1\}^N$ synchronously by
$$
\sigma_i(t + 1) = f_i(\sigma_{j_1(i)}(t), \dots, \sigma_{j_{K_i}(i)}(t)) , \qquad i = 1, \dots, N .
$$
An **attractor** is a cycle $\boldsymbol\sigma^{(1)} \to \boldsymbol\sigma^{(2)} \to \dots \to \boldsymbol\sigma^{(L)} \to \boldsymbol\sigma^{(1)}$ of the update, of **length** $L$ (a
**fixpoint** when $L = 1$), and its **basin** is the set of states whose orbits reach it. The **Kauffman model** ($N$-$K$ model) with bias $p$ draws, once and for all, for each node
$K$ distinct controlling elements uniformly at random and a coupling function whose $2^K$ table entries are independently $0$ with probability $p$ and $1$ with probability $1 - p$.
:::

::::

The state space has $2^N$ elements, so every orbit is eventually periodic and the state space splits into the basins of finitely many attractors. `RandomBooleanNetworkSystem` draws a
Kauffman network; its argument `bias` is the probability that a table entry is $1$, that is $1 - p$ in Gros's notation, which changes nothing in the formulas below because they
depend on $p(1 - p)$. Its table is indexed by the inputs read as a binary number, the first input being the most significant bit. `YeastCellCycleSystem` is the eleven-protein network of
the budding yeast cell cycle that Gros discusses [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.5.2].

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is Gros's network of three sites. It is small enough to list all eight states.

::: {#exm-bn-gros-three}
#### Gros's three-site network

In Gros's Fig. 7.3, $\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 \land \sigma_3$, $\sigma_2 = \sigma_1 \lor \sigma_3$ and $\sigma_3 = \sigma_1 \lor \sigma_2$ [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.2.3,
Fig. 7.3]. The eight states form one cycle of length $2$ and two fixpoints, and the fixpoint $111$ is reached from $5$ of the $8$ states, the probability $5/8$ that Gros gives
[@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.4.1].

```{.python .run}
import itertools
def step(s):
    a, b, c = s
    return (b & c, a | c, a | b)
for s in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=3):
    print("".join(map(str, s)), "->", "".join(map(str, step(s))))
def attractor(s):
    seen = []
    while s not in seen:
        seen.append(s)
        s = step(s)
    return tuple(sorted(seen[seen.index(s):]))
basins = {}
for s in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=3):
    basins.setdefault(attractor(s), []).append(s)
print({tuple("".join(map(str, q)) for q in a): len(b) for a, b in basins.items()})
```

```{.text .run-output}
000 -> 000
001 -> 010
010 -> 001
011 -> 111
100 -> 011
101 -> 011
110 -> 011
111 -> 111
{('000',): 1, ('001', '010'): 2, ('111',): 5}
```
:::

The coupling functions of $K$ inputs are many. Gros counts $2^{2^K}$ of them [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.2.2, eq. (7.3)].

::: {#exm-bn-function-count}
#### Counting coupling functions

A function on the $2^K$ input combinations assigns $0$ or $1$ to each: $2^{2^K}$ functions, $2$, $4$, $16$ and $256$ for $K = 0, 1, 2, 3$. For $K = 1$ they are the two constants, the
identity and the negation; for $K = 3$ they include Gros's examples of a canalizing function, the majority function and the generalized XOR [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.2.1,
Table 7.1].
:::

Loops of nodes with one input each can be solved by hand. Gros treats the loop of three sites with identities [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.4.2].

::: {#exm-bn-identity-loop}
#### A loop of identities

With $\sigma_1 \leftarrow \sigma_3$, $\sigma_2 \leftarrow \sigma_1$, $\sigma_3 \leftarrow \sigma_2$, the state rotates: $ABC \to CAB \to BCA$. The states $000$ and $111$ are fixpoints, and the
other six form two cycles of length $3$, $100 \to 010 \to 001$ and $011 \to 101 \to 110$.
:::

Negations change the cycle lengths. With all three couplings negations, Gros finds one cycle of length $2$ and one of length $6$ [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.4.2].

::: {#exm-bn-negation-loop}
#### A loop of negations

The map $ABC \to \bar C\bar A\bar B$ has the cycle $000 \to 111 \to 000$, and the other six states form one cycle of length $6$. The run lists the cycles.

```{.python .run}
import itertools
step = lambda s: (1 - s[2], 1 - s[0], 1 - s[1])
seen, cycles = set(), []
for s in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=3):
    if s in seen:
        continue
    orbit = [s]
    while (s := step(s)) != orbit[0]:
        orbit.append(s)
    seen |= set(orbit)
    cycles.append(["".join(map(str, q)) for q in orbit])
print(cycles)
```

```{.text .run-output}
[['000', '111'], ['001', '011', '010', '110', '100', '101']]
```
:::

A constant coupling function breaks a loop. Gros's example is the loop with the functions $0$, $1$ and the identity [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.4.2, eq. (7.21)].

::: {#exm-bn-constant}
#### A global fixpoint

With $\sigma_1 = 0$, $\sigma_2 = \sigma_1$ and $\sigma_3 = 1$, any state goes to $0A1$ and then to $001$, which is fixed: its basin is the whole state space. In a long loop of the $K = 1$ Kauffman
net, the chance that some coupling is constant is high, which keeps the cycles of $K = 1$ networks short.
:::

Separate modules combine their cycles. Gros's network of five sites has two loops of identities, of three and two sites [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.4.2].

::: {#exm-bn-five-site}
#### Two loops

The loop $A \to B \to C \to A$ has cycles of lengths $1$ and $3$, the loop $D \to E \to D$ of lengths $1$ and $2$, so the network has fixpoints such as $00000$ and $11111$, cycles of length $3$ such as
$10000 \to 01000 \to 00100$, of length $2$, and of length $6$ such as the one through $10010$, the least common multiple of $3$ and $2$.

```{.python .run}
import collections
import itertools
step = lambda s: (s[2], s[0], s[1], s[4], s[3])
seen, lengths = set(), collections.Counter()
for s in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=5):
    if s in seen:
        continue
    orbit = [s]
    while (s := step(s)) != orbit[0]:
        orbit.append(s)
    seen |= set(orbit)
    lengths[len(orbit)] += 1
print("number of cycles of each length:", dict(sorted(lengths.items())))
```

```{.text .run-output}
number of cycles of each length: {1: 4, 2: 2, 3: 4, 6: 2}
```
:::

The package's networks are found exhaustively for small $N$. Every state is mapped once, and the cycles of the resulting map are the attractors.

::: {#exm-bn-package-attractors}
#### Attractors of a Kauffman network

For one network of `RandomBooleanNetworkSystem` with $N = 12$ and $K = 2$, the successor of each of the $4096$ states is computed from the package's wiring and tables, and the cycles of the
successor map are listed with their basins. This network has a cycle of length $2$ with a basin of $3732$ states and one of length $5$ with the remaining $364$.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.systems.biology.systems_biology import RandomBooleanNetworkSystem
N, K = 12, 2
system = RandomBooleanNetworkSystem(N, K, random_state=5).prepare().system_
inputs = np.array([[int(n.split("_")[1]) for n in f.inputs] for f in system.interactions])
tables = np.array([f.table for f in system.interactions])
X = (np.arange(2 ** N)[:, None] >> np.arange(N)) & 1
code = sum(X[:, inputs[:, k]] << (K - 1 - k) for k in range(K))
succ = tables[np.arange(N), code] @ (1 << np.arange(N))
attractor = {}
for s in range(2 ** N):
    path = []
    while s not in path:
        path.append(s)
        s = int(succ[s])
    cycle = path[path.index(s):]
    key = min(cycle)
    attractor.setdefault(key, [len(cycle), 0])[1] += 1
print("attractors (length, basin):", sorted(attractor.values()))
```

```{.text .run-output}
attractors (length, basin): [[2, 3732], [5, 364]]
```
:::

The number and length of attractors depend on $K$. Averages over twenty networks with $N = 12$ show more and longer cycles as $K$ grows, the trend that the phase diagram explains.

::: {#exm-bn-k-dependence}
#### Attractors against connectivity

For $K = 1$ the networks have about two attractors of length about one, for $K = 2$ slightly more and longer ones, and for $K = 3$, $4$ and $12$ (every node reads every other) more attractors than for
$K \leq 2$ and much longer cycles, the mean length growing steadily with $K$. Gros's random-walk estimate for $K = N$ gives about $\frac N2\ln 2 \approx 4.2$ cycles plus a constant [@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.4.4, eq. (7.26)].

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.systems.biology.systems_biology import RandomBooleanNetworkSystem
N = 12
X = (np.arange(2 ** N)[:, None] >> np.arange(N)) & 1
def cycle_lengths(succ):
    state, out = np.zeros(len(succ), dtype=np.int8), []
    for s in range(len(succ)):
        path = []
        while state[s] == 0:
            state[s] = 1
            path.append(s)
            s = int(succ[s])
        if state[s] == 1:
            out.append(len(path) - path.index(s))
        for q in path:
            state[q] = 2
    return out
for K in (1, 2, 3, 4, 12):
    counts, lengths = [], []
    for seed in range(20):
        system = RandomBooleanNetworkSystem(N, K, random_state=seed).prepare().system_
        inputs = np.array([[int(n.split("_")[1]) for n in f.inputs] for f in system.interactions])
        tables = np.array([f.table for f in system.interactions])
        code = sum(X[:, inputs[:, k]] << (K - 1 - k) for k in range(K))
        c = cycle_lengths(tables[np.arange(N), code] @ (1 << np.arange(N)))
        counts.append(len(c))
        lengths.append(np.mean(c))
    print(f"K = {K}: mean number of attractors {np.mean(counts):.2f}, mean length {np.mean(lengths):.2f}")
```

```{.text .run-output}
K = 1: mean number of attractors 2.00, mean length 1.30
K = 2: mean number of attractors 2.30, mean length 2.11
K = 3: mean number of attractors 3.80, mean length 4.89
K = 4: mean number of attractors 3.35, mean length 7.09
K = 12: mean number of attractors 5.55, mean length 17.87
```
:::

The yeast cell cycle network is the showcase application. Its eleven proteins switch on or off by the sign of their summed activations and inhibitions
[@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.5.2, eq. (7.29)].

::: {#exm-bn-yeast}
#### The attractors of the yeast network

All $2^{11} = 2048$ states of the network flow into $7$ fixpoints. The largest basin has $1764$ states, $86\%$ of the state space, and its fixpoint has Cdh1 and Sic1 on and all other proteins off,
the biological G1 state. Gros reports the $7$ fixpoints and the basin of $1764$ states; the percentage printed beside it, $72\%$, does not match that count
[@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.5.2].

```{.python .run}
import itertools
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.systems.biology.systems_biology._boolean import YEAST_DECAYING, YEAST_INPUTS, YEAST_NODES
index = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(YEAST_NODES)}
W = np.zeros((11, 11))
for node, inputs in YEAST_INPUTS.items():
    for source, weight in inputs:
        W[index[node], index[source]] = weight
decays = np.array([n in YEAST_DECAYING for n in YEAST_NODES])
X = np.array(list(itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=11)))
def step(X):
    a = X @ W.T
    return np.where(a > 0, 1, np.where(a < 0, 0, np.where(decays, 0, X)))
for _ in range(50):
    X = step(X)
fixpoints, basins = np.unique(X, axis=0, return_counts=True)
print("fixpoints:", len(fixpoints), "; basin sizes:", sorted(basins.tolist(), reverse=True))
print("largest basin's fixpoint:", [n for n, v in zip(YEAST_NODES, fixpoints[basins.argmax()]) if v])
```

```{.text .run-output}
fixpoints: 7 ; basin sizes: [1764, 151, 109, 9, 7, 7, 1]
largest basin's fixpoint: ['Cdh1', 'Sic1']
```
:::

The cell cycle itself is a trajectory into that attractor. Started from G1 with the cell-size signal Cln3 switched on, the network passes through the known phases and returns to G1 in $12$ steps
[@grosComplexAdaptiveDynamical2015, Sec. 7.5.2, Fig. 7.13].

::: {#exm-bn-yeast-cycle}
#### The cell-cycle trajectory

`YeastCellCycleSystem` starts with Cln3, Cdh1 and Sic1 on. The run prints the active proteins at each step until the state repeats.

```{.python .run}
import numpy as np
from skcomplex.core.engine.runtime import simulate
from skcomplex.systems.biology.systems_biology import YeastCellCycleSystem
from skcomplex.systems.biology.systems_biology._boolean import YEAST_NODES
run = simulate(YeastCellCycleSystem(), until=14)
states = np.array([np.asarray(run.get_values(f"{n}.x")) for n in YEAST_NODES]).T.astype(int)
for t, s in enumerate(states):
    print(t, [n for n, v in zip(YEAST_NODES, s) if v])
    if t > 0 and (s == states[t - 1]).all():
        break
```
